summary: VITA is a hands-free health-monitoring station for astronauts. From one medical record per crew member, the astronaut controls the system with hand gestures (no touching shared screens) and runs seven daily checks: blood pressure, heart rate, emotional state, body temperature, BMI with a camera-guided exercise routine, ocular fatigue and radiation dose. Each check ends in a clear report: the data obtained with reference ranges, observations explained in plain language, and recommendations split into “act now”, “prevent” and “improve”. Fatigue is measured with a low-cost ESP32-CAM that tracks the eye (smooth pursuit, reflexes and PERCLOS). The radiation module replays a real solar storm from NASA DONKI and shows how much dose the astronaut avoids by reaching the shelter in time. Everything is saved locally, plotted in the record, and turned into daily habits with streaks, badges and reminders, so medical self-monitoring becomes routine instead of an afterthought on long missions.
details:
What it does. VITA is a local medical station for space crews. Each astronaut has a medical record with personal data, a photo, a daily-progress panel and charts. Opening the record leads to a menu with seven color-coded modules arranged around a central camera. The astronaut moves a hand to point and closes the fist to “click”, so the station can be used without touching keyboards or shared screens — useful with gloves, in microgravity and for hygiene in a closed habitat.

The seven modules

Blood pressure – ASTRA monitor: live monitoring, Bluetooth cuffs (standard GATT profile), manual entry or an experimental camera-based estimate calibrated against a cuff.

Heart rate – photoplethysmography (PPG) with the fingertip on the camera, Bluetooth heart-rate sensors or manual entry; the ESP32-CAM light can be adjusted with W/S.

Emotional assistant (AstroMind) – stress, sleep, mood and social connection give a wellbeing index; guided 4-7-8 breathing and anti-stress binaural audio are built in.

Body temperature – a physiological thermal engine (core, tympanic, forehead, axillary and distal temperatures, sweating, vascular tone and shivering) shown as a live thermal map. It is ready for a real IR sensor.

BMI + exercise routine – pose detection registers the body silhouette, then counts 10 squats and 10 shoulder presses, measuring depth and range of motion. Resistance exercise is the main countermeasure against bone and muscle loss in microgravity.

Ocular fatigue index – an ESP32-CAM tracks the iris during a smooth-pursuit test, a saccadic-reflex test and PERCLOS (eyelid closure). It includes image enhancement, adaptive blink detection, filtering, live signal-quality feedback and automatic recalibration, and ends with a fatigue level and an eye-exercise protocol.

Radiation dosimeter – a mission dosimeter based on real solar storms of May 2024 (NASA DONKI). An animated scene shows what happens outside the ship and inside it. Comparing the four shelter decisions (go immediately, 30 min late, 2 h late or not at all) shows the dose avoided, and the mission total is tracked against the NASA career limit (600 mSv, NASA-STD-3001).

After every check, VITA produces a report:

the data obtained, with reference ranges;

observations, each with a “what does it mean?” explanation;

a comparison with the previous measurement;

recommendations grouped as act now, prevent and improve wellbeing.

The results feed the medical record, whose charts show only real measurements: a new astronaut starts blank.

Making health a habit. Daily goal, streaks, experience points and badges (Bronze → Legendary) encourage daily checks. Reminder pop-ups on the crew screen show who still has pending checks and how much time is left in the day.

Benefits. VITA turns scattered measurements into one longitudinal record per astronaut. Early trends become visible: rising blood pressure, chronic sleep debt, fatigue, dose build-up. The crew gets explanations and countermeasures instead of bare numbers. It runs locally, without depending on the link to Earth, and uses low-cost hardware (laptop webcam, ESP32-CAM, optional Bluetooth sensors).

How we built it.

Python (Flask server, OpenCV, MediaPipe face/hand/pose landmarkers, NumPy, Streamlit, pandas, Plotly).

JavaScript (Canvas animations, Web Audio, Web Bluetooth, camera API), HTML and CSS.

ESP32-CAM firmware in C++ (Arduino).

Each health subsystem was developed by a different team member and integrated as an independent module with a common loading screen, execution flow and reporting engine.

Limitations. VITA is a research prototype and not a medical device. Temperature and some vital-sign scenarios use simulated physiological models until real sensors are connected. The camera-based blood-pressure value is an experimental estimate. Reference ranges are guidance for training and must be validated by flight surgeons.

Next steps. Connect clinical-grade sensors (IR thermometer, cuff, pulse oximeter), validate the fatigue and PPG methods against reference devices, and add secure sync with the flight surgeon when the link is available.
